ety.text: From Middle English nobody, no-body, no body. By surface analysis, no (“none, not any”, adjective) + body (“one, person, individual”).

senses.d: Not any person; the logical negation of somebody.
ex: I asked several people, but nobody knew how.
As nobody who is not blind can have failed to notice, I had my hair cut just yesterday.

senses.d: Something that has no body or an especially small one.

ety.text: From Latin nē (“not”) + ipse (emphatic, literally “himself”) + ūnus (“one”), by surface analysis “not even one”. Cognate with Neapolitan nisciuno, Sardinian nisciunu, Friulian nissun, Ligurian nisciǜn, and Old French neisune. Compare Spanish ninguno and Romanian niciun.

Inherited from Old Spanish nadi, nade (“no one”), inherited from Latin nātī (“born men/people”), perfect past participle of nāscor (“to be born”), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-. ety.text: From Middle English noble, from Old French noble, borrowed from Latin nōbilis (“knowable, known, well-known, famous, celebrated, high-born, of noble birth, excellent”), from nōscere, gnōscere (“to know”). False cognate of Arabic نبيل (nabīl). Displaced native Middle English athel, from Old English æþele.

senses.d: An aristocrat; one of aristocratic blood.
ex: This country house was occupied by nobles in the 16th century.

senses.d: A medieval gold coin of England in the 14th and 15th centuries, usually valued at 6s 8d.
ex: I lyked no thynge his playe, / For yf I had not quyckely fledde the touche, / He had plucte oute the nobles of my pouche.
And who shall then stick closest to ye, and excite others? not he who takes up armes for cote and conduct, and his four nobles of Danegelt.

senses.d: Having honorable qualities; having moral eminence and freedom from anything petty, mean or dubious in conduct and character.
ex: He is a noble man who would never put his family in jeopardy.

senses.d: Of exalted rank; of or relating to the nobility; distinguished from the masses by birth, station, or title; highborn.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French noble, borrowed from Latin nōbilis according to the TLFi dictionary.
From Old Galician-Portuguese nobre, from Latin nōbilis (“noble”), from nōscō (“to know; to recognise”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-.
From Old French nobilité, from Latin nobilitas. Equivalent to noble + -ity.

senses.d: A noble or privileged social class, historically accompanied by a hereditary title; aristocracy.
ex: The castle was once home to the Scottish nobility.
Titles of nobility were passed down through generations.
He displayed nobility of character when helping his rivals.

ety.text: From Old Italian nobilità, nobilitade, nobilitate, from Latin nōbilitātem (“fame; nobility”).
